etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English envious, from Anglo-Norman envious, from Old French envieus, envious (modern French envieux), from Latin invidiōsus; more at envy. Doublet of invidious, borrowed directly from Latin. Displaced native Old English æfestiġ.

definitions.definition: Feeling or exhibiting envy; jealously desiring the excellence or good fortune of another; maliciously grudging

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Psalms 37:1:
quote.text: Fret not thy ſelfe becauſe of euill doers, neither bee thou enuious againſt the workers of iniquitie.

quote.citation: 1827, [John Keble], The Christian Year: Thoughts in Verse for the Sundays and Holydays throughout the Year, volume (please specify |volume=I or II), Oxford, Oxfordshire:  […]  [B]y W. Baxter, for J. Parker; and C[harles] and J[ohn] Rivington, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: My soul is envious of mine eye.

quote.citation: 1651, Jer[emy] Taylor, The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living. […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  Francis Ashe […], →OCLC:
quote.text: for no man was ever so amorous, as to love a toad; none so envious, as to repine at the condition of the miserable

quote.citation: 1593, [William Shakespeare], Venus and Adonis, London:  […]  Richard Field, […], →OCLC:
